Ittingen
IT-ing-un
n. (the Thurgau charterhouse sacked and burnt by a reforming mob in 1524)
From a Germanic personal name with the settlement ending -ingen.

Definition · Webster 1828 · Scriptures · Corruption · Roots · Usage · Related

Biblical Definition

Ittingen in the Thurgau was an Augustinian house that became a charterhouse in 1461. In July 1524 a crowd from the surrounding villages and from Zurich territory, stirred up by preaching against the mass and by a local grievance over an arrested preacher, broke into the charterhouse, drank the cellar dry, burnt the archives and the library and set fire to the buildings. The Ittinger Sturm became a political crisis for Zurich, which had to disown and punish the rioters, and it is one of the uglier episodes of the Swiss Reformation. The house was rebuilt and survived until 1848. This dictionary records Ittingen because the sin it illustrates is a Protestant one and the correction is biblical. Zeal without knowledge is named, “they have a zeal of God, but not according to knowledge” (Rom 10:2). Haste is condemned in the same terms, “he that hasteth with his feet sinneth” (Pro 19:2). Men will do violence thinking it service, “whosoever killeth you will think that he doeth God service” (Joh 16:2), and the Lord rebuked disciples who wanted fire from heaven, “Ye know not what manner of spirit ye are of” (Luk 9:55).

Webster 1828 Definition

Webster (1828) defines zeal as passionate ardour in pursuit of an object; a riot as a tumultuous disturbance by an unlawful assembly; iconoclasm as the breaking of images; sacrilege as the violation of sacred things; and rashness as the quality of acting without due deliberation.

expand to see more

ZEAL, n. Passionate ardor in the pursuit of any thing; in general, this word is used in a good sense, but it may denote enthusiasm or ardor in a bad cause.

RIOT, n. In a general sense, tumult; uproar; hence technically, a tumultuous disturbance of the public peace by an unlawful assembly of three or more persons.

ICONOCLAST, n. A breaker or destroyer of images; one who attempts to reform without regard to established usages.

SACRILEGE, n. The crime of violating or profaning sacred things; the alienating to common purposes what has been appropriated to religious uses.

RASHNESS, n. The quality of being rash, or of acting or speaking without due deliberation; precipitation; inconsiderate haste.

Key Scripture

Rom 10:2 — "For I bear them record that they have a zeal of God, but not according to knowledge."

Pro 19:2 — "Also, that the soul be without knowledge, it is not good; and he that hasteth with his feet sinneth."

Joh 16:2 — "They shall put you out of the synagogues: yea, the time cometh, that whosoever killeth you will think that he doeth God service."

Luk 9:55 — "But he turned, and rebuked them, and said, Ye know not what manner of spirit ye are of."

Modern Corruption

Thurgau charterhouse sacked and burnt by a reforming mob in 1524, in an episode Zurich itself had to disown and punish.

expand to see more

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is that Paul credits his opponents with real zeal and still calls them wrong, which is the only honest way to describe the Ittinger mob, “For I bear them record that they have a zeal of God, but not according to knowledge” (Rom 10:2). Solomon states the general rule about acting faster than one understands, “he that hasteth with his feet sinneth” (Pro 19:2).

The second thing is how convincing such violence feels from inside. The Lord warns that persecutors will be sincere, “whosoever killeth you will think that he doeth God service” (Joh 16:2), and he turned on two of his own disciples when they proposed to burn a Samaritan village in his name, “Ye know not what manner of spirit ye are of” (Luk 9:55). A Reformation whose doctrine this dictionary holds produced, on one July night in the Thurgau, a drunken mob burning a library. The principle to recover is that the rightness of a cause does not sanctify its methods.

Greek & Hebrew Roots

Greek zelos (G2205), zeal; Greek epignosis (G1922), full knowledge; Hebrew 'uts (H213), to hasten; Greek latreia (G2999), service; Greek epitimao (G2008), to rebuke.

expand to see more

Greek zelos (G2205) — zeal, real but misdirected; “they have a zeal of God, but not according to knowledge”, Romans 10:2.

Greek epignosis (G1922) — knowledge, the missing thing; “but not according to knowledge”, Romans 10:2.

Hebrew 'uts (H213) — to press, to hasten; “he that hasteth with his feet sinneth”, Proverbs 19:2.

Greek latreia (G2999) — religious service, sincerely offered; “will think that he doeth God service”, John 16:2.

Greek epitimao (G2008) — to rebuke, as he rebuked them; “Ye know not what manner of spirit ye are of”, Luke 9:55.

Usage

"“they have a zeal of God, but not according to knowledge” (Rom 10:2) — zeal credited and still called wrong."

"“will think that he doeth God service” (Joh 16:2) — how convincing it feels from inside."

"“Ye know not what manner of spirit ye are of” (Luk 9:55) — said to his own disciples."
